p.src: As for Walter, in a few days he had become one of the masters of the world—a financier more omnipotent than a king. He was no longer the Jew, Walter, the director of a bank, the proprietor of a yellow newspaper; he was M. Walter the wealthy Israelite, and he wished to prove it.

p.src: Knowing the straitened circumstances of the Prince de Carlsbourg who owned one of the fairest mansions on Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore, he proposed to buy it. He offered three million francs for it. The prince, tempted by the sum, accepted his offer; the next day, Walter took possession of his new dwelling. Then another idea occurred to him—an idea of conquering all Paris—an idea a la Bonaparte.

p.src: At that time everyone was raving over a painting by the Hungarian, Karl Marcovitch, exhibited by Jacques Lenoble and representing "Christ Walking on the Water." Art critics enthusiastically declared it to be the most magnificent painting of the age. Walter bought it, thereby causing entire Paris to talk of him, to envy him, to censure or approve his action. He issued an announcement in the papers that everyone was invited to come on a certain evening to see it.

p.src: Du Roy was jealous of M. Walter's success. He had thought himself wealthy with the five hundred thousand francs extorted from his wife, and now he felt poor as he compared his paltry fortune with the shower of millions around him. His envious rage increased daily. He cherished ill will toward everyone—toward the Walters, even toward his wife, and above all toward the man who had deceived him, made use of him, and who dined twice a week at his house. Georges acted as his secretary, agent, mouthpiece, and when he wrote at his dictation, he felt a mad desire to strangle him.

p.src: Laroche reigned supreme in the Du Roy household, having taken the place of Count de Vaudrec; he spoke to the servants as if he were their master. Georges submitted to it all, like a dog which wishes to bite and dares not. But he was often harsh and brutal to Madeleine, who merely shrugged her shoulders and treated him as one would a fretful child. She was surprised, too, at his constant ill humor, and said: "I do not understand you. You are always complaining. Your position is excellent."

p.src: His only reply was to turn his back upon her. He declared that he would not attend M. Walter's fete—that he would not cross the miserable Jew's threshold. For two months Mme. Walter had written to him daily, beseeching him to come to see her, to appoint a meeting where he would, in order that she might give him the seventy thousand francs she had made for him. He did not reply and threw her letters into the fire. Not that he would have refused to accept his share of the profits, but he enjoyed treating her scornfully, trampling her under foot; she was too wealthy; he would be inflexible.

One always acts too hastily—one never reflects sufficiently." And longing, bitter longing possessed him, corrupting all his pleasure, rendering life odious.

p.src: She seized his hand, kissed it passionately, and fled toward the house. He returned more leisurely, and entered the conservatory with head erect and smiling lips. His wife and Laroche were no longer there. The crowd had grown thinner. Suzanne, leaning on her sister's arm, advanced toward him. In a few moments, Rose, whom they teased about a certain Count, turned upon her heel and left them.

p.src: Du Roy, finding himself alone with Suzanne, said in a caressing voice: "Listen, my dear little one; do you really consider me a friend?"

p.src: "Why, yes, Bel-Ami."

p.src: "You have faith in me?"

u.src: "You have faith in me?"

p.src: "Perfect faith."

p.src: "Do you remember what I said to you a while since?"

u.src: "Do you remember what I said to you a while since?"

p.src: "About what?"

u.src: "About what?"

p.src: "About your marriage, or rather the man you would marry."

u.src: "About your marriage, or rather the man you would marry."

p.src: "Yes."

u.src: "Yes."

p.src: "Well, will you promise me one thing?"

u.src: "Well, will you promise me one thing?"

p.src: "Yes; what is it?"

u.src: "Yes; what is it?"

p.src: "To consult me when you receive a proposal and to accept no one without asking my advice."

u.src: "To consult me when you receive a proposal and to accept no one without asking my advice."

p.src: "Yes, I will gladly."

u.src: "Yes, I will gladly."

p.src: "And it is to be a secret between us—not a word to your father or mother."

p.src: "Not a word."

p.src: Rival approached them saying: "Mademoiselle, your father wants you in the ballroom."

p.src: She said: "Come, Bel-Ami," but he refused, for he had decided to leave at once, wishing to be alone with his thoughts. He went in search of his wife, and found her drinking chocolate at the buffet with two strange men. She introduced her husband without naming them.

p.src: In a short while, he asked: "Shall we go?"

p.src: She took his arm and they passed through the almost deserted rooms.

p.src: Madeleine asked: "Where is Mme. Walter; I should like to bid her good-bye."

p.src: "It is unnecessary. She would try to keep us in the ballroom, and I have had enough."

p.src: "You are right."

p.src: On the way home they did not speak. But when they had entered their room, Madeleine, without even taking off her veil, said to him with a smile: "I have a surprise for you."

p.src: He growled ill-naturedly: "What is it?"

p.src: "Guess."

p.src: "I cannot make the effort."

p.src: "The day after to-morrow is the first of January."

p.src: "It is the season for New Year's gifts."

p.src: "Here is yours, which Laroche handed me just now." She gave him a small black box which resembled a jewel-casket.

p.src: He opened it indifferently and saw the cross of the Legion of Honor. He turned a trifle pale, then smiled, and said: "I should have preferred ten millions. That did not cost him much."

p.src: She had expected a transport of delight and was irritated by his indifference.

p.src: "You are incomprehensible. Nothing seems to satisfy you."

p.src: He replied calmly: "That man is only paying his debts; he owes me a great deal more."

p.src: She was astonished at his tone, and said: "It is very nice, however, at your age."

p.src: He took the casket, placed it on the mantelpiece, and looked for some minutes at the brilliant star within it, then he closed it with a shrug of his shoulders and began to prepare to retire.

p.src: "L'Officiel" of January 1 announced that M. Prosper Georges du Roy had been decorated with the Legion of Honor for exceptional services. The name was written in two words, and that afforded Georges more pleasure than the decoration itself.

p.src: An hour after having read that notice, he received a note from Mme. Walter, inviting him to come and bring his wife to dine with them that evening, to celebrate his distinction.

p.src: At first he hesitated, then throwing the letter in the fire, he said to Madeleine: "We shall dine at the Walters' this evening."

p.src: In her surprise she exclaimed: "Why, I thought you would never set your foot in their house again."

p.src: When they arrived at Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore, they found Mme. Walter alone in the dainty boudoir in which she received her intimate friends. She was dressed in black and her hair was powdered. At a distance she appeared like an old lady, in proximity, like a youthful one.

u.src: When they arrived at Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore, they found Mme. Walter alone in the dainty boudoir in which she received her intimate friends.
She was dressed in black and her hair was powdered.
At a distance she appeared like an old lady, in proximity, like a youthful one.

p.src: "Are you in mourning?" asked, Madeleine.

u.src: "Are you in mourning?" asked, Madeleine.

p.src: She replied sadly: "Yes and no. I have lost none of my relatives, but I have arrived at an age when one should wear somber colors. I wear it to-day to inaugurate it; hitherto I have worn it in my heart."

p.src: The dinner was somewhat tedious. Suzanne alone talked incessantly. Rose seemed preoccupied. The journalist was overwhelmed with congratulations, after the meal, when all repaired to the drawing-rooms. Mme. Walter detained him as they were about to enter the salon, saying: "I will never speak of anything to you again, only come to see me, Georges. It is impossible for me to live without you. I see you, I feel you, in my heart all day and all night. It is as if I had drunk a poison which preyed upon me. I cannot bear it. I would rather be as an old woman to you. I powdered my hair for that reason to-night; but come here—come from time to time as a friend."

p.src: Walter, who had preceded them, with his two daughters and Madeleine, awaited Du Roy near the picture of "Christ Walking on the Water."

u.src: Walter, who had preceded them, with his two daughters and Madeleine, awaited Du Roy near the picture of "Christ Walking on the Water."

p.src: "Only think," said he, "I found my wife yesterday kneeling before that painting as if in a chapel. She was praying!"

u.src: "Only think," said he, "I found my wife yesterday kneeling before that painting as if in a chapel.
She was praying!"

p.src: Mme. Walter replied in a firm voice, in a voice in which vibrated a secret exaltation: "That Christ will save my soul. He gives me fresh courage and strength every time that I look at Him." And pausing before the picture, she murmured: "How beautiful He is! How frightened those men are, and how they love Him! Look at His head, His eyes, how simple and supernatural He is at the same time!"

p.src: Suzanne cried: "Why, He looks like you, Bel-Ami! I am sure He looks like you. The resemblance is striking."

p.src: She made him stand beside the painting and everyone recognized the likeness. Du Roy was embarrassed. Walter thought it very singular; Madeleine, with a smile, remarked that Jesus looked more manly. Mme. Walter stood by motionless, staring fixedly at her lover's face, her cheeks as white as her hair.
